openObligations: The complete actual published article pages 900-904 and complete PMC author main text, both figures and Table 1 were read. The downloaded six-page university PDF includes an additional references page and adjacent article text; only the identified CETCH article supplies evidence.

The supplement containing detailed Methods, supplementary text, Figures S1-S14 and Tables S1-S8 was not read. Archive files were HTML challenges; publisher access failed and the author repository exposes only a publisher link. Complete buffer, temperature, enzyme preparation, calibration, raw mass spectra, replicate counts and supplementary controls remain outside reconstruction.

The admitted case is a supplied and externally assembled in vitro enzyme network. Mature enzymes, cofactors, chemical starting acceptor and resource/regeneration inputs are supplied; it does not synthesize its enzyme catalysts, produce an autonomous cell, or demonstrate collectively autocatalytic production of all network components.

Stepwise conversion in CETCH 1.0 did not establish continuous cycling: the simultaneously combined version stalled before a complete turn at methylsuccinyl-CoA. The main text attributes this to electron-acceptor limitations; the underlying supplementary controls are not newly verified.

CETCH 5.4 has 13 named core reactions plus auxiliary proofreading/cofactor regeneration, with 17 enzymes from nine organisms in the complete source system. Reaction count, enzyme count and biological origins are distinct; they are not universal carrier minima or independently verified assembly stoichiometry.

The principal evidence combines six intermediate abundance/isotopologue time courses with a source-topology interpretation and a coupled malate assay. Glyoxylate is trapped by supplied malate synthase using externally added acetyl-CoA. Malate contains externally supplied carbon and is not itself a product composed solely of the fixed CO2.

Source Figure 2C reports 540 micromolar malate over 90 minutes, corresponding in its two-CO2-per-glyoxylate stoichiometric accounting to 1080 micromolar fixed CO2. The cited approximately 5 nmol CO2 per minute per mg uses core cycle protein, not all supplied proteins. These are source-reported values, not independently reproduced quantities or uncertainties.

Progressive 13C enrichment constrains repeated pathway passage under the declared topology. It does not directly track every individual molecule, prove a global steady state, reveal all side fluxes, certify complete mass balance or establish unbounded throughput. Finite intermediate levels change over the same assay.

Thermodynamic profiles, ATP equivalents and hypothetical photon costs in Table 1 are calculations under adopted stoichiometry, P/O and photophosphorylation assumptions. No calorimetry, complete energy balance, realized photosynthetic coupling or universal energetic superiority follows.

Different CETCH versions alter enzymes, regeneration, protection and side-reaction handling together. No isolated allosteric feedback variable, universally adaptive stabilization mechanism, matched direct comparison with a natural in vivo cycle, or unique causal contribution of each change is admitted.

No long-term robustness under varying conditions, homeostatic flux control, adaptive persistence, membrane transport, autonomous catalyst replacement, origin-of-life sequence or universal requirement for a prior autocatalytic RNA network is measured.
No raw HPLC-MS data replay, model fitting, calibration reconstruction, independent acquisition or laboratory optimization is claimed.

limitations: Purified, already synthesized clients and purified E. coli GroEL/SR1/GroES are studied in vitro. The selected data do not observe translation, cellular stress adaptation, protein damage surveillance, routing to proteasomes or organismal proteome reliability.

Adding the GroEL/GroES/ATP protocol is a combined intervention. These panels do not by themselves isolate ATP hydrolysis, individual ATPase steps, capture specificity, every component necessity or all possible active folding effects.

Activity recovery, tryptophan fluorescence, light scattering and size-exclusion elution measure different properties. None alone supplies an atomic native structure, a unique folding path or the fraction of every chain in a single native state.
All readouts and fitted rates come from one publication. No raw traces, new fit, covariance, curve digitization, independent replication or analytically-checked status is supplied.

The source interprets these conditions through aggregation prevention. Its broad passive-cage conclusion is retained as conditional, not a proof that all chaperonins are passive or that no client can experience an active conformational effect.

Rubisco activity requires native-dimer formation. SR1 aliquots are chilled to release GroES and allow released monomers to assemble before the enzyme assay; the readout does not show active Rubisco dimers inside the single-client cis chamber.
Figure 1B compares refolding Rubisco plus BSA with native Rubisco plus BSA and BSA alone in solution; it does not directly measure a matched light-scattering reduction inside GroEL/SR1.

Figure 1 C source inference permits reversible intermediate-sized association plus growth of persistent void-volume material. The data do not show that every aggregate dissolves or that all solution aggregation is reversible.

BSA is a controlled solution additive at 7.5 micromolar, not a missing universal chaperone or a universal concentration threshold. Reported rate constants are apparent source fits without newly reconstructed errors.

The DM-MBP client is mature V8G/Y283D maltose-binding protein. Tryptophan fluorescence is an environment-sensitive refolding proxy; no maltose-binding affinity, transport activity or enzymatic client assay is measured here.

The chloride-deficient protocol uses 100 mM Hepes pH7.5,20 mM KOAc and 5 mM Mg(OAc)2 after dilution from 9.5 M urea. Buffer, salt concentration/anion and starting denaturant all change; chloride alone is not isolated.

Concentration dependence and light scattering support intermolecular association under the tested solution protocol. They do not identify a unique oligomer structure or prove that every fluorescence intermediate is an aggregate.

Rate equivalence in the changed solution protocol constrains a need for a faster intrinsic cage-only step for this client under those conditions. It does not prove an unchanged microscopic route or universal absence of chaperonin active effects.

contexts.observable: Radiochemical Rubisco activity, dynamic light scattering and 35S size-fractionation versus refolding time
contexts.preparation: Use purified R. rubrum Rubisco at 80 nM and 15 C. Dilute100-fold from 5 M guanidine-HCl,100 mM Tris-HCl pH7.5,1 mM EDTA and 20 mM DTT into 50 mM Tris-HCl pH7.7,10 mM KCl,7 mM MgCl2 and 2 mM DTT, with or without 7.5 micromolar BSA. For chaperonin arms include 2 micromolar GroEL or SR1 during capture, then add 2.5 micromolar GroES and 5 mM ATP. Quench timed aliquots with hexokinase/glucose and assay radiochemical Rubisco activity. SR1 aliquots receive4 C for 10 min to release GroES and permit dimerization. Separately monitor dynamic light scattering and Superose6 elution of 35S-labeled Rubisco in the solution-plus-BSA reaction, with native/BSA controls.

contexts.preparation: Use purified mature DM-MBP V8G/Y283D, normally100 nM at 25 C, plus concentration-series and wild-type controls. The chloride-containing arm dilutes100-fold from 6 M guanidine-HCl into 20 mM Tris-HCl pH7.5,200 mM KCl and 5 mM Mg(OAc)2. The chloride-deficient arm dilutes100-fold from 9.5 M urea into 100 mM Hepes pH7.5,20 mM KOAc and 5 mM Mg(OAc)2. In each chaperonin arm capture with 250 nM GroEL or SR1, then add 250 nM GroES and 5 mM ATP. Record tryptophan fluorescence at 295 nm excitation/345 nm emission and separate dynamic light scattering. The two solution protocols differ in several components.

rationale.statement: For these Rubisco and DM-MBP preparations the source evidence supports aggregation as a competing solution fate and chaperonin-dependent recovery under the declared protocols. DM-MBP rate equivalence after changing the solution protocol limits a necessary cage-only acceleration account for that comparison. The source passive-cage interpretation remains conditional; no universal identity of microscopic folding paths or absence of active chaperonin effects follows.
